title: Hanuman makes himself small
hookLine: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean calls himself the weakest of the army
carry: hanuman's humility: small self, big hope
last: MARYADA: THE RIGHT WAY MATTERS, NOT JUST THE RESCUE.

lines: THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.
cards: Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Goodbyes like this are the hardest part: you're leaving, they're staying, and you want to say something that lasts after you've gone.
Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.

teach.h: THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.
teach.b: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know.

One day at Chitrakuta a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power; the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet.
Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says plainly that she can hold on only for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her.
Don't grieve. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon with Sugriva's army. And because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he adds something surprising.

teach.h: NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.
teach.b: There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas calls himself the least of the army.
If he's the strongest, the rescue hangs on one monkey. If he's the weakest, help is enormous, and coming.
He makes himself small, so her hope can be large. This is the Hanuman devotees love most: the strongest one in the story, and the humblest.

In Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, when Rama later praises him, Hanuman says it was all Rama's power, none of his own. In Hindu devotion, humility means getting the ego out of the way so something bigger can come through.
And it's one reason many families read this book, the Sundara Kanda, aloud when someone is sick or in trouble: it's the book where hope comes back.

how: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in times of illness or trouble, and devotees love Hanuman as both the strongest and the humblest of Rama's servants; the chudamani is a familiar image in Ramayana art.

games.q: you're Hanuman. Sita fears no army could cross this sea. you just did it alone. what do you tell her?
o: only I could do it, so it's hopeless.
many in the army are stronger than me, and none weaker.
games.why: Hanuman calls himself the least of Sugriva's army, so that Sita sees the rescue as certain, not a one-monkey miracle.

practice: If you pray, hold in mind someone waiting on something hard, a diagnosis, a result, a return, and say Hanuman's name or a short prayer for them, the way families read the Sundara Kanda for someone in trouble.
If you don't pray, hold them in mind and let a few simple, true words of comfort form, shaped to what they most fear, not to what makes you look good. Breathe them slowly in and out.

wordCard.voice: Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.

orig.note: Sanskrit cūḍāmaṇi, crest jewel: cūḍā, the crown of the head, and maṇi, jewel.
